paper_metadata.title: Quantum-inspired variational algorithms for partial differential equations: Application to financial derivative pricing

summary: The paper proposes a quantum‑inspired variational Monte Carlo solver using autoregressive neural‑network quantum states for high‑dimensional PDEs. Experiments solve diffusion and Black–Scholes equations on grids up to n=16 (2^16 mesh points), reporting relative errors below ~15% and claiming a classical runtime crossover with Euler finite-difference around n≈16. All results are obtained using classical neural networks and Monte Carlo sampling, with no gate‑based quantum hardware or circuits.

experiments.description: Variational quantum Monte Carlo / neural-network quantum state solver for the d-dimensional heat equation (diffusion) with Gaussian initial conditions, benchmarked against forward Euler time-stepping.

algorithm.variant: Variational Monte Carlo with autoregressive neural-network quantum states; McLachlan variational principle; mesh-based PDE solver
algorithm.ansatz: autoregressive neural-network quantum state (MADE-style masked fully connected network)
algorithm.optimizer: Adam for pre-training; linear solve with SVD-based regularized update during evolution
algorithm.convergence_criteria: pre-training for 50k iterations; evolution run for total time T=1 with fixed step size

hyperparameters.learning_rate_schedule: warm-start for first 1/10 of total training iterations, then decayed by factor 10 at 3/7 and 5/7 of total training iterations
hyperparameters.problem_sizes_reported: n up to 16 qubits; dimensions d=1..9; n/d=4 or 5

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Pre-trained to match the initial condition using random mesh-point batches; initial variational parameters selected by minimizing ||α0|ψβ0⟩ - |u0⟩||^2

optimizer_settings.learning_rate_schedule: warm-start then step decays at 3/7 and 5/7

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Spatially discretized PDE state on a regular grid with 2^n grid points mapped to an n-qubit computational basis state; each basis state corresponds to a mesh point x_k
problem_formulation.objective_function: Approximate solution of ∂_t u(t,x)=D∇·∇u(t,x) using McLachlan variational principle; minimize ||Φ_{t+δt}^t(u_θ)-u_{θ+δθ}||^2 leading to M δθ = V δt
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Boundary conditions implemented via source functions; Dirichlet and periodic boundary conditions considered

problem_instance.description: High-dimensional diffusion/heat equation with Gaussian initial condition; compared to forward Euler and used to demonstrate scaling with dimension

dataset_specification.description: Regular hypercube mesh; Gaussian initial condition defined via modified Bessel function expression; periodic or Dirichlet boundary conditions

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Discretize domain into 2^n grid points; use mesh-based representation; pre-train on randomly selected mesh points
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Averaged across exactly 5 seeds; relative error computed against forward Euler solution over space-time history; running time measured over 2k iterations

implementation_details.classical_solver: Forward Euler finite-difference method as baseline; SVD regularization for solving the linear update system
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Mesh discretization; autoregressive sampling; per-sample gradient extraction with BackPack; CPU parallel extraction of sparse operator rows
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Relative error computation against Euler baseline; option-pricing mapping discussed later in paper

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: not reported; convergence visualized in snapshots and error tables

results.unit: relative error threshold mentioned in text

speedup_claims.conditions: for the mesh-based PDE solver as dimension d grows; paper states forward Euler scales as O(T×2^(2n)) while the proposed method scales as O(TB poly(n))
speedup_claims.caveats: The proposed method has higher constant overhead and uses approximate stochastic updates; the paper also notes implicit access to state entries rather than O(1) lookup.

speedup_claims.conditions: reported in the running-time analysis for diffusion experiments
speedup_claims.caveats: This is based on the paper’s reported timing table; Euler could not be run for higher dimensions due to memory constraints.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(TB poly(n)); forward pass O(TBn^2), sampling O(TBn^3)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(T×2^(2n)) for forward Euler as stated in the paper
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: n=16 qubits (paper states method is already faster than forward Euler for n=16)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Paper claims runtime crossover with Euler around n≈16 (2^16 grid points) in Table 2, but this comparison is purely classical.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not applicable; no quantum hardware or circuit resources defined.
limiting_factors: Algorithm is purely classical (quantum-inspired VMC with neural-network quantum states).
No gate-based circuit, qubits, or quantum measurements implemented.
Performance comparison is between two classical solvers (VMC vs. Euler finite difference).

notes: No actual quantum hardware or gate-level circuit is used; this is a quantum-inspired/classical VMC-style algorithm. num_qubits inferred from the mesh encoding statement: 2^n grid points mapped to an n-qubit state, with experiments up to n=16.
circuit_depth is not applicable in the usual gate-based sense; the paper reports algorithmic scaling and autoregressive sampling complexity, not a quantum circuit depth.
All experiments run with classical neural networks and Monte Carlo sampling.
No quantum hardware or circuit-level implementation exists, so quantum advantage cannot be evaluated.

experiments.description: Variational quantum Monte Carlo / neural-network quantum state solver applied to multi-asset Black-Scholes option pricing, including 1D European call and 2D basket/rainbow/spread options.

algorithm.variant: Variational Monte Carlo with autoregressive neural-network quantum states for Black-Scholes PDE via heat-equation transformation
algorithm.ansatz: autoregressive neural-network quantum state (MADE-style masked fully connected network)
algorithm.optimizer: Adam for pre-training; linear solve with SVD-based regularized update during evolution
algorithm.convergence_criteria: pre-training and evolution run to expiry time T; no explicit stopping criterion beyond fixed iterations/time horizon
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Same pre-training procedure as diffusion experiment; initial condition set by discounted payoff on the transformed heat-equation domain

optimizer_settings.learning_rate_schedule: warm-start then step decays at 3/7 and 5/7

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Spatial discretization of transformed heat-equation state on a regular grid mapped to an n-qubit basis state; used to represent option value over the mesh
problem_formulation.objective_function: Solve the Black-Scholes PDE (after transformation to a heat equation) for European option pricing; minimize McLachlan variational residual as in the diffusion experiment
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Boundary values imposed using time-discounted payoff functions on the hypercube faces

problem_instance.description: European option pricing under the multi-asset Black-Scholes model; includes 1D call option benchmark and 2D basket call, basket put, rainbow max call, and spread put options

dataset_specification.description: Synthetic Black-Scholes parameters; payoffs listed in Table 3; 1D analytic Black-Scholes formula used as ground truth

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Transform Black-Scholes PDE to heat equation via change of variables; truncate positive orthant to a hypercube domain; use discounted payoff boundary conditions
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: 1D: compare against analytic Black-Scholes formula and forward Euler; 2D: compare against forward Euler; dimensionality ablation shown for d=1,2,3,5

implementation_details.classical_solver: Forward Euler finite-difference method as baseline; analytic Black-Scholes formula in 1D
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Heat-equation transformation of Black-Scholes PDE; domain truncation to hypercube; boundary payoff approximation
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Option price extraction at expiry; relative error against analytic or Euler solutions; convexity plot versus strike price

convergence_data.loss_curve_shape: not reported; results summarized in Table 4 and Figure 3/4

speedup_claims.conditions: for the transformed heat-equation solver used for Black-Scholes pricing as dimension increases
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper emphasizes the same complexity tradeoff as in the diffusion experiment; no separate asymptotic proof is given for pricing beyond the shared solver.
The paper reports accuracy against the analytic formula but does not claim a speedup over the closed-form solution.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: O(TB poly(n)); forward pass O(TBn^2), sampling O(TBn^3)
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: O(T×2^(2n)) for forward Euler as stated in the paper
complexity_analysis.crossover_n: n=16 qubits (stated in diffusion section; no separate crossover reported for pricing)

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not applicable; option-pricing experiments use the same classical solver.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Not applicable; no quantum circuit implementation.
limiting_factors: Method remains classical even in the financial application.
Evaluation compares to analytic Black–Scholes solution and classical Euler PDE solver.
No quantum hardware, simulator, or circuit resources reported.

notes: No actual gate-based quantum hardware is used; this is a quantum-inspired classical VMC solver. num_qubits inferred from the same mesh-to-n-qubit encoding used throughout the paper.
circuit_depth is not applicable in the usual gate-based sense; the paper reports algorithmic scaling and not a quantum circuit depth.
Option-pricing section applies the same classical VMC/NQS solver.
Comparisons are only against classical baselines.
